rows.what: The program you double-click. It checks our server for a newer version, downloads updates, and starts the game. It shows you what it is doing at every step.
rows.sent: It asks our server for the version list and the update; it sends nothing about you or your game. Our server's web log sees your IP address and the time, like any website

rows.what: The launcher's settings: the address of our update server, the public key it uses to check that an update really came from us, your version, and whether to check for updates. You can read it in Notepad. Setting check_enabled = false turns update checks off.
The project's read-me (today the full developer README, about 0.6 MB) and the version of this build.

The game itself. Every update replaces this folder completely, so never keep your own files in it. Contains ostrog.exe (the game program), ostrog.pck (the game's art, sounds and scripts), hf_godot.dll (the game's simulation engine) and copies of README.md and VERSION.

The launcher's own folder. logs/launcher.log is a plain diary of what the launcher did ("checked for updates", "downloaded version X", "you cancelled the download"); it stays on your computer and grows by about half a kilobyte each time you start Ostrog. .keep is an empty placeholder.
rows.delete: The log, yes. Leave the rest

rows.what: Used during an update: the new version being unpacked, and a copy of your previous version so an update that fails to start can be undone. Emptied once the new version has started; the empty folder may stay.
rows.delete: Yes, when no update is running

sections.title: Your saved games and settings
sections.where: %APPDATA%\Godot\app_userdata\Ostrog\ (type that into the Explorer address bar)

rows.what: Your options: sound, interface scale, camera and so on.
Which alerts you chose to see or pause on.

Your saved games: the rolling autosaves (auto.0.hfsave to auto.2.hfsave) and your manual save (manual.hfsave). Each save is a folder holding world.bin, chronicle.sqlite and manifest.json; it is written first as <name>.hfsave.tmp so a half-written save never replaces a good one. While a save is being written the folder also holds .ostrog-save-writing, a tiny marker the launcher looks for so an update never starts mid-save; it disappears when the save is done.
rows.delete: No: this is your game. Delete only to start over

rows.what: The game engine's own diary, godot.log, used to find crashes. The engine also keeps a few older ones from earlier launches, named godot<date>T<time>.log, and removes the oldest itself.
The engine's store of graphics programs it has already prepared for your graphics card, so the next start is quicker (under 1 MB).

A detailed record of why each person did what they did. Only written when debug mode is on. It grows quickly (about 6 MB in four minutes at the fastest speed); at 32 MB it is renamed ostrog-debug.log.1 and a new one starts, so the two together never pass about 64 MB.

Only if you turn Timelapse on: one picture of the egress point at noon each game day, with a small note of what happened, kept per world so you can watch it grow. At most 120 pictures and 160 MB per world, for at most 6 worlds (about 1 GB in the worst case); the oldest are removed first.

While a game is open, the egress point's history is kept in a working file here (chronicle-<number>.sqlite, with -wal and -shm companions) instead of in memory; your saves copy it. The game removes the file when it closes and clears any left over from a crash on a later start. The empty folder stays.
rows.delete: Yes, when the game is not running

rows.what: While the launcher downloads an update: the part-downloaded file, checked before anything is installed and removed when the launcher has finished with it. If the launcher is closed in the middle of a download, the part file stays until you delete it.
rows.delete: Yes, when no update is running
